modelResponse.episodeSummary: George Antonelli, Sinus Bradycardia, warning, hemodynamically stable but symptomatic
keyECGEvidence: morphology: Sinus P waves with prolonged PR; narrow QRS; scooped ST segments; prolonged QTc 510 ms; U waves present
modelResponse.mechanism: Increased vagal tone and direct myocardial depression due to excessive digoxin levels.
contributingFactors: Amiodarone interaction with digoxin (amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein, reducing digoxin clearance)
Potential amiodarone effect on conduction system
Underlying sinus node dysfunction exacerbated by medications

rejectedAlternatives.why: While possible given age and history, the markedly elevated digoxin level (2.4 ng/mL TOXIC) and classic ECG findings (scooped ST segments, prolonged PR, U waves) strongly point to digoxin toxicity as the primary driver of the bradycardia.

Amiodarone can cause bradycardia, but the ECG morphology (scooped ST segments, U waves) is more characteristic of digoxin effect. While amiodarone contributes to the overall picture and interacts with digoxin, the digoxin level is clearly toxic and explains the specific ECG changes.
The INR is CRITICAL HIGH (5.8), but this does not directly cause bradycardia. It is a separate critical issue requiring management but is not the etiology of the current rhythm.

recommendedActions: Administer Atropine 0.5 mg IV push if symptomatic bradycardia persists or worsens
Administer Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind) given toxic level (2.4 ng/mL) and symptoms (nausea, muscle aches)
Monitor potassium closely (hypokalemia can worsen digoxin toxicity)
uncertainty: Exact contribution of amiodarone to bradycardia is difficult to isolate from digoxin toxicity.
Presence of underlying sinus node dysfunction cannot be fully excluded.
